issues.legal_issue: A constitutional challenge to the Speaker’s certification of a bill as a Money Bill is subject to judicial review when it alleges constitutional illegality, although that review is highly restricted.
material_facts: The Finance Act was certified as a Money Bill despite containing provisions that amended laws governing the structure and service conditions of multiple tribunals.
The petitioners challenged the certification as unconstitutional, arguing that the tribunal-related provisions did not fall within the constitutional definition of a Money Bill.
issues.conclusion: The certification is not immune from judicial review. Review is limited to exceptional cases involving gross unconstitutionality or blatant substantial illegality, with a presumption of legality and judicial deference in favour of the Speaker’s decision.
issues.legal_principle: Articles 110(3) and 122(1) do not bar review of a certification alleged to violate the Constitution; Article 122 protects against challenges based on procedural irregularity, not substantive illegality or unconstitutionality. The Court relied on Raja Ram Pal v. Lok Sabha, Union of India v. Jyoti Prakash Mitter and the majority in K.S. Puttaswamy v. Union of India. It stated that Mohd. Saeed Siddiqui v. State of Uttar Pradesh and Yogendra Kumar Jaiswal v. State of Bihar could not be relied on insofar as they placed the Speaker’s decision beyond judicial review.

predicates.money_bill_certification_challenged: A party challenges the Speaker’s certification of a bill as a Money Bill.
predicates.alleged_constitutional_illegality: The challenge alleges that the certification breaches the constitutional scheme, rather than merely identifying a procedural irregularity.

issues.definition: When a party challenges a Money Bill certification for constitutional illegality, the certification may be reviewed by a court within a highly restricted scope.

issues.legal_issue: The constitutional validity of certifying the tribunal-related provisions in the Finance Act as a Money Bill required consideration by a larger Bench.
material_facts: The challenged enactment included provisions abolishing or merging tribunals, changing tribunal members’ service conditions, and delegating related rule-making powers.
The petitioners contended that these provisions were not Money Bill provisions or matters incidental to them.

The Court found that the governing principles for interpreting Article 110(1), including the effect of the word “only” and the treatment of provisions that do not conform to that Article, required clarification.
issues.conclusion: The question of whether the relevant provisions of the Finance Act were validly enacted as a Money Bill was referred to a larger Bench; the Court did not decide the merits of that question.
issues.legal_principle: Article 110(1) defines a Money Bill by reference to provisions dealing only with the specified subjects and incidental matters. The Court considered the majority decision in K.S. Puttaswamy v. Union of India but found that it did not sufficiently clarify the scope of Article 110(1) for the issues raised. Because the present Bench was of equal strength and identified a need for authoritative clarification, the question was referred to a larger Bench.

predicates.money_bill_validity_challenged: A party contests whether a bill was constitutionally eligible to be passed as a Money Bill.
predicates.tribunal_amendments_in_certified_bill: The certified bill contains provisions changing the organisation or service conditions of tribunals.
predicates.article_110_scope_requires_clarification: The applicable principles for deciding whether the bill’s provisions fit the constitutional Money Bill definition require authoritative clarification.

issues.definition: When the validity of a Money Bill certification is contested, the bill changes tribunal arrangements, and the constitutional test requires clarification, the validity question is referred to a larger Bench.

issues.legal_issue: Delegating authority to prescribe tribunal members’ qualifications and service conditions is not excessive where the governing legislative policy and binding constitutional principles sufficiently guide the delegate.
material_facts: The legislation authorised the Central Government to make rules on tribunal members’ qualifications, appointments, tenure, remuneration, resignation, removal and other service conditions.
The legislation set maximum tenure and age limits and prohibited disadvantageous changes to service conditions after appointment.
The governing tribunal statutes and this Court’s prior decisions supplied principles concerning tribunal independence and the necessary qualifications and protections of members.
issues.conclusion: The delegation did not suffer from excessive delegation of legislative functions.
issues.legal_principle: The legislature must retain essential legislative functions, including determining policy, but may delegate ancillary details where the legislative policy and standards provide sufficient guidance. The Court relied on In re Delhi Laws Act; B. Shama Rao v. Union Territory of Pondicherry; Ramesh Birch v. Union of India; Devi Das Gopal Krishnan v. State of Punjab; Municipal Corporation of Delhi v. Birla Cotton; M.K. Papiah & Sons v. Excise Commissioner; Registrar of Cooperative Societies v. K. Kunjabmu; Keshavlal Khemchand and Son Pvt. Ltd. v. Union of India; and Gwalior Rayon Silk Mfg. Co. v. Assistant Commissioner of Sales. It held that the objectives of the parent enactments and the binding principles in R.K. Jain, L. Chandra Kumar, Union of India v. R. Gandhi, Madras Bar Association and Gujarat Urja Vikas Ltd. guide the rule-maker.

predicates.tribunal_service_conditions_delegated: The legislature authorises the executive to prescribe details of tribunal members’ qualifications, appointments or service conditions.
predicates.governing_policy_and_binding_principles_: The legislation and binding judicial principles provide standards that guide the executive’s exercise of the delegated authority.

issues.definition: Delegating details of tribunal service conditions is not excessive when legislative policy and binding principles guide how the executive may exercise that authority.

issues.legal_issue: Rules governing tribunal appointments, qualifications, removals and tenure are invalid when their combined effect undermines judicial independence and the judicial character of adjudication.
material_facts: The rules gave the Executive a predominant role in search-cum-selection committees, with little or no judicial participation in several appointments.

The rules allowed people without adjudicatory experience to hold judicial or presiding positions and permitted technical members without the necessary judicial experience to perform adjudicatory functions.
The rules gave the Executive a significant role in removing tribunal members, including through inquiry arrangements lacking adequate judicial safeguards.
The rules imposed short tenures, including a three-year term, and contained inconsistent retirement ages and other service conditions.
issues.conclusion: The 2017 Tribunal Rules were contrary to the parent enactment and constitutional principles, and were struck down in their entirety. The Central Government was directed to formulate replacement rules in accordance with the Court’s decisions and principles.
issues.legal_principle: Tribunals exercising judicial functions must have independence, judicially dominant appointment processes, members with qualifications commensurate with the jurisdiction transferred to them, and adequate security of tenure and removal safeguards. Technical members may be appointed where specialised expertise is needed, but cannot replace judicial members where adjudication requires judicial experience. The Court relied on Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala; R.K. Jain v. Union of India; L. Chandra Kumar v. Union of India; Union of India v. R. Gandhi; Madras Bar Association v. Union of India (2014 and 2015); Supreme Court Advocates-on-Record Association v. Union of India; and Gujarat Urja Vikas Ltd. v. Essar Power Ltd.

predicates.tribunal_service_rules_challenged: A proceeding challenges rules governing the appointment or service conditions of tribunal members.
predicates.executive_dominates_appointments: The Executive controls tribunal selection committees without adequate judicial participation.
predicates.judicial_roles_open_to_unqualified_membe: The rules permit people lacking the legal qualifications or adjudicatory experience required for the transferred judicial work to decide disputes.
predicates.executive_controls_removal_without_judic: The Executive can remove tribunal members without adequate judicial involvement or equivalent safeguards.
predicates.tenure_and_service_terms_weaken_independ: Short or inconsistent tenure and service conditions undermine members’ independence or deter qualified candidates.

issues.definition: When challenged tribunal service rules permit executive dominance, inadequately qualified adjudicators, insufficient removal safeguards, or independence-undermining service terms, the rules are invalidated.

issues.legal_issue: Tribunals must have financial independence from ministries or departments that may appear before them as litigants.
material_facts: Tribunals were administered by sponsoring or parent ministries and could depend on those ministries for finances, infrastructure and other operational needs.
A sponsoring ministry or department could itself be a litigant before the tribunal it administered.
The Court considered that dependence for day-to-day requirements could compromise perceived or actual tribunal independence.
issues.conclusion: The Ministry of Finance was directed, in consultation with the relevant nodal ministry or department, to earmark separate and dedicated funds for tribunals, with their operating expenditure charged on the Consolidated Fund of India. Tribunals should not depend on a litigant ministry for day-to-day requirements.
issues.legal_principle: Tribunals must be institutionally and financially independent, particularly from a department that is a party before them. L. Chandra Kumar v. Union of India called for independent oversight and a single nodal ministry pending an independent agency; Union of India v. Madras Bar Association also criticised tribunal dependence on sponsoring departments. The Court held that the essential requirement is financial independence and that the identity of the nodal agency is less important than tribunals’ ability to function without seeking their day-to-day needs from it.

predicates.tribunal_administered_by_litigant_depart: A ministry or department that administers a tribunal may also litigate before it.
predicates.tribunal_depends_on_department_for_opera: The tribunal relies on that ministry or department for funding needed for its ordinary operations.

issues.definition: When a tribunal is administered by a department that litigates before it and depends on that department for operating funds, dedicated funding must protect its independence.

issues.legal_issue: A judicial impact assessment is required to evaluate the effects of tribunal legislation and ensure adequate resources for tribunals.
material_facts: The legislation made extensive changes to tribunal structures and service conditions without an assessment of their effects on judicial workload or resource needs.
The changes could increase litigation and add to the Judiciary’s burden, while tribunals also required adequate staffing, infrastructure and funding.
The petitioners sought an assessment of the effects of legislation on the judicial system.
issues.conclusion: The Ministry of Law and Justice was directed to conduct a judicial impact assessment of the tribunals affected by the Finance Act and submit its findings to the competent legislative authority. The Union was also directed to assess tribunals’ financial and resource requirements and provide sufficient resources.
issues.legal_principle: Legislatures and the Executive should assess the likely effects of legislation on courts, tribunals, caseloads, staffing and infrastructure. The Court relied on Salem Advocate Bar Association (II) v. Union of India and the report of the committee constituted pursuant to that decision, which addressed legislative assessment of additional cases, courts, judges, staff and infrastructure.

predicates.tribunal_legislation_changes_adjudicator: Legislation changes tribunals or the adjudicatory work assigned to them.
predicates.judicial_and_resource_effects_not_assess: The effects on litigation, judicial workload, staffing, infrastructure or funding have not been assessed.

issues.definition: When legislation changes the tribunal framework without assessing its effects on adjudication and resources, a judicial impact assessment is required.

issues.legal_issue: Tribunal members cannot be accorded the constitutional rank and status of Supreme Court or High Court judges merely because their pay or perquisites are equivalent.
material_facts: Some tribunal chairpersons, presidents or members had been given pay, perquisites or status equivalent to those of constitutional court judges.
The Court considered that tribunals are statutory bodies and supplemental to constitutional courts, even when staffed by retired judges.
issues.conclusion: Pay or perquisite equivalence does not confer equivalent constitutional rank or status on tribunal members. The Government could provide in new rules that tribunal officers do not hold such equivalent rank or status merely on the basis of equal pay or perquisites.
issues.legal_principle: The constitutional position of judges derives from their constitutional office and cannot be conferred on statutory tribunal members merely through executive action, legislation, salary or perquisites. The Court relied on T.N. Seshan v. Union of India and L. Chandra Kumar v. Union of India, which described tribunals as supplemental rather than substitutes for superior courts.

predicates.statutory_tribunal_officer_given_equal_p: A statutory tribunal officer receives pay or perquisites equivalent to those of a constitutional court judge.

issues.definition: When a statutory tribunal officer receives equal pay or perquisites, that equality alone does not give the officer constitutional rank.

issues.legal_issue: Direct statutory appeals from tribunals to the Supreme Court require reconsideration because they burden the Court and bypass High Court review.
material_facts: Numerous statutes allowed direct appeals to the Supreme Court from tribunal decisions.
The Court found that such appeals contributed to its docket burden, reduced time for constitutional work, and made access to justice more difficult for some litigants.
The direct-appeal provisions could bypass the High Courts and deprive their judges of experience in specialised areas.
issues.conclusion: The Union was directed, in consultation with the Law Commission or another expert body, to revisit the relevant statutory provisions and place proposals before Parliament for consideration of whether direct appeals should be removed and High Court appeals provided where appropriate.
issues.legal_principle: The constitutional design preserves High Court judicial review under Articles 226 and 227, and direct statutory appeals can undermine access to justice and the Supreme Court’s constitutional role. The Court relied on L. Chandra Kumar v. Union of India; R.K. Jain v. Union of India; Madras Bar Association v. Union of India (2014); Gujarat Urja Vikas Ltd. v. Essar Power Ltd.; Mafatlal Industries Ltd. v. Union of India; Sangram Singh v. Election Tribunal; Union of India v. Major General Shrikant Sharma; and the Law Commission’s 272nd Report. The Court did not invalidate the direct-appeal provisions in this proceeding; it directed that they be reconsidered.

predicates.tribunal_orders_directly_appealable_to_s: A statute provides a direct appeal to the Supreme Court from a tribunal decision.
predicates.direct_appeals_burden_supreme_court_or_b: The direct appeal contributes to the Supreme Court’s burden or bypasses High Court review.

issues.definition: When statutory direct appeals from tribunals burden the Supreme Court or bypass High Courts, those appeal provisions must be reconsidered.

issues.legal_issue: Tribunals should be rationalised and amalgamated where appropriate, with benches located to provide access to justice and meet caseload needs.
material_facts: The tribunal system had uneven caseloads: some tribunals faced substantial backlogs while others had relatively few matters.
Some tribunals were located at only one place, while other tribunals faced resource and personnel pressures.
The uneven distribution and overlapping subject matter impaired effective use of resources and access to justice.
issues.conclusion: The Union was directed to rationalise and amalgamate tribunals based on subject-matter homogeneity and to establish an adequate number of benches commensurate with existing and anticipated workloads, including circuit benches at the seats of major jurisdictional High Courts.
issues.legal_principle: Tribunals must be effective, competent and accessible alternatives that use resources efficiently. Their organisation and locations should reflect subject-matter commonality, caseload and litigants’ access to justice. The Court relied on the Law Commission’s 272nd Report and its decisions in Madras Bar Association v. Union of India.

predicates.tribunals_have_uneven_caseloads_or_overl: Different tribunals have materially uneven workloads or deal with sufficiently similar subject matter to permit rationalisation.
predicates.tribunal_locations_impede_access: The location or number of tribunal benches makes access to adjudication difficult for litigants.

issues.definition: When tribunal workloads or subject matter are uneven and tribunal locations impede access, the system must be rationalised and accessible benches provided.
